en: The Sūtra on the Summit of Mount Gayā, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Bodhiruci of India during the Northern Wei Dynasty:
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Bhagavān was staying at Mount Gayā in the city of Gayā.

When the Tathāgata first attained enlightenment, he was accompanied by a great assembly of bhikṣus numbering one thousand; they had all previously been brahmins with matted hair who had completed what was to be done, accomplished their task, laid down the heavy burden, achieved their own benefit, exhausted the fetters of existence, attained liberation of mind through right knowledge, gained mastery over all states of mind, and had reached the further shore—all were arhats.

There were also immeasurable and boundless bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who had gathered from the worlds of the ten directions, possessing great majesty and virtue, having attained all the patiences (kṣānti), dhāraṇīs, and profound samādhis, and endowed with all supernatural powers (abhijñā). Their names were as follows:

Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva, Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, Mahāsthāmaprāpta Bodhisattva, Gandhahasti Bodhisattva, Śūradatta Bodhisattva, Śūraprabha-jñāna Bodhisattva, and others served as their leaders; such bodhisattva-mahāsattvas were immeasurable in number.
They were surrounded by a great assembly including devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, non-humans, and others.
At that time, the World-Honored One, alone and in solitude, entered the profound samādhi of all Buddhas. Observing the dharma-realm, he had this thought:

"I have attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and acquired all-encompassing wisdom. What was to be done has been accomplished; I have laid down the heavy burden and crossed over the perilous paths of existence. I have extinguished ignorance and attained true illumination; I have extracted the arrows and severed craving. I have completed the Dharma-boat, struck the Dharma-drum, blown the Dharma-conch, and raised the Dharma-banner. I have turned the seed of birth-and-death to reveal the nature of nirvāṇa; I have blocked off the evil paths and opened the straight road; I have departed from the fields of transgression and revealed the field of merit."
I shall now examine those dharmas: who attains anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, and by what kind of wisdom does one attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?
What is this Dharma of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi that is realized?
Is it attained by means of the body,
or is it attained by means of the mind?

If it were attained by means of the body, the body would be without knowledge and without sensation, like grass, like wood, like a clod of earth, or like a shadow; it would have no consciousness, being composed of the four great elements, born of father and mother, and its nature is impermanent;
it exists only through the support of clothing, food and drink, bedding, and bathing, yet this phenomenon must inevitably return to decay, ruin, and extinction.

If it were attained by means of the mind, the mind would be like an illusion, arising from various conditions; it has no location, no characteristics, no substance, and nothingness. "Bodhi" exists only as a name spoken for the sake of conventional truth;

it has no sound, no form, no accomplishment, no activity, and no entry. It cannot be seen and cannot be relied upon; the paths of coming and going are severed; it transcends all verbal expression and emerges from the triple world. It is without seeing, hearing, cognition, attachment, or observation; it is free from conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), without contention, and without demonstration. It cannot be scrutinized or perceived; it is without resonance and without letters, having departed from the path of language. By what kind of wisdom can one thus realize Bodhi?

Regarding the Dharma of enlightenment realized by one who realizes bodhi: such dharmas exist only as names, are spoken of only as provisional designations, are spoken of only as composite names, and are spoken of based on conventional names. They are explained through non-discriminative discrimination; they are provisionally established yet not established, without substance and detached from substance, without grasping and ineffable. There is no attachment there, no person who realizes, no means of realization, and no dharma that can be realized. To penetrate thus is called attaining *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; it is without difference and detached from difference, and it has no characteristic of bodhi.
At that time, Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta stood to the right of the Buddha in the great assembly, holding a great precious parasol to shade the Buddha from above.
Then, Mañjuśrī, silently knowing the thoughts in the World-Honored One’s mind, addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
"If awakening has such characteristics, how should sons and daughters of good family resolve their minds and abide in awakening?
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī:
"Sons and daughters of good family should resolve their minds and abide in accordance with those very characteristics of awakening."
Mañjuśrī said: “World-Honored One,
how should one know the characteristic of bodhi?”
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī:

"As for the characteristic of bodhi, it transcends the triple world and surpasses all worldly names and language; it surpasses all echoes, being without the arousal of the thought of enlightenment and the extinction of all such arousals—this is the dwelling of the arousal of the bodhicitta."
Therefore, Mañjuśrī! When all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas transcend all forms of aspiration, this is the stage of the resolve for awakening (cittotpāda-vihāra). Mañjuśrī!
Non-arising is the dwelling of the arousal of the bodhicitta.
Mañjuśrī! For one who has aroused the bodhicitta, there is no object of arousal; this is the dwelling of the arousal of the bodhicitta.
Mañjuśrī! The dwelling of one who has resolved upon bodhicitta is the dwelling of unimpededness; this is the dwelling of one who has resolved upon bodhicitta. Mañjuśrī!
One who generates the bodhicitta abides in accordance with the nature of phenomena (dharmatā); this is the dwelling of generating the bodhicitta. Mañjuśrī!
One who generates the bodhicitta does not cling to any phenomena; this is the dwelling of generating the bodhicitta.
Mañjuśrī! One who gives rise to the bodhicitta does not destroy the reality-limit (bhūtakoṭi); this is the dwelling of one who has given rise to the bodhicitta. Mañjuśrī!
To generate the bodhicitta is to be without shifting, without adding, without difference, and without unity; this is the dwelling of generating the bodhicitta. Mañjuśrī!

One who generates the bodhicitta should dwell having generated it in this way: like a reflection in a mirror, like a mirage in the heat, like a shadow, like an echo, like space, and like the moon in water. Thus should one dwell having generated the bodhicitta.
At that time, there was a son of the gods in the assembly named Candraprabhaśrī, who had attained non-retrogression from the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. He asked Mañjuśrī:
"By first contemplating what dharma do the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the bodhisattva conduct?"
"By relying on what dharma does one practice the bodhisattva conduct? Mañjuśrī replied, "O Devaputra!"
"The practice of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas takes great compassion as its foundation for the sake of all sentient beings.
The devaputra then asked Mañjuśrī,
"What does the great compassion of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas take as its foundation?"
Mañjuśrī replied: "Devaputra!
The great compassion of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas has a straightforward mind as its foundation."
The devaputra again asked Mañjuśrī,
“What is the foundation of the straightforward mind of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas? Mañjuśrī replied:
“O Son of Heaven!
The straightforward mind of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas has the mind of equality toward all sentient beings as its foundation.
The Son of Heaven then asked Mañjuśrī:
“What is the basis for the impartial mind that bodhisattva-mahāsattvas maintain toward all sentient beings? Mañjuśrī replied,
“O Devaputra!...”
“The impartial mind toward all sentient beings held by bodhisattva-mahāsattvas has non-differentiation and the departure from differentiation as its basis.
The devaputra then asked Mañjuśrī,
“What is the basis for the non-differentiation and departure from differentiation in the practice of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas?”
Mañjuśrī replied, “Devaputra!
The practice of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas is non-dual and free from duality, having the profound and pure mind as its foundation.”
The devaputra again asked Mañjuśrī,
“What is the foundation of the profound and pure mind of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas? Mañjuśrī replied:
“Devaputra! The profound and pure mind of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas has the mind of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi as its foundation.
The Devaputra then asked Mañjuśrī:
“What serves as the basis for the mind of unexcelled, perfect enlightenment of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas?
Mañjuśrī replied, “O Devaputra!”
"The minds of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas directed toward anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi take the six pāramitās as their foundation.
The devaputra then asked Mañjuśrī,
"What do the six pāramitās of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas take as their foundation?"
Mañjuśrī replied: "O Devaputra!
For all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, the six pāramitās have skillful means and wisdom as their foundation."
The devaputra again asked Mañjuśrī,
“What is the basis for the skillful means and wisdom of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas? Mañjuśrī replied:
“Devaputra! The skillful means and wisdom of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have heedfulness as their foundation.
The devaputra then asked Mañjuśrī:
“What is the foundation for the non-negligence of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas? Mañjuśrī replied, “O Devaputra!”
"All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice non-negligence by taking the three types of wholesome conduct as their foundation.
The celestial son then asked Mañjuśrī,
"What serves as the foundation for the three types of wholesome conduct of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas?"
Mañjuśrī replied: "Devaputra!
The three types of wholesome conduct of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have the ten paths of wholesome action as their foundation."
The devaputra again asked Mañjuśrī,
“What is the basis for the ten paths of wholesome action of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas? Mañjuśrī replied:
“Devaputra! For all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, the ten paths of wholesome action have the observance of ethical discipline as their foundation.
The Devaputra then asked Mañjuśrī:
“What is the foundation upon which the precepts of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are based? Mañjuśrī replied,
“O Devaputra!...”
"The precept-keeping of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas has right mindfulness as its foundation.
The devaputra then asked Mañjuśrī,
"What is the foundation of the right mindfulness of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas?"
Mañjuśrī replied: “Devaputra!
For all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, right mindfulness has right observation as its foundation.”
The devaputra again asked Mañjuśrī,
“What serves as the basis for the correct contemplation of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas? Mañjuśrī replied:
“Devaputra! The correct contemplation of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas has firm mindfulness and non-forgetfulness as its foundation.
The Devaputra then asked Mañjuśrī:
“How many kinds of minds do bodhisattva-mahāsattvas possess that can accomplish the cause and accomplish the fruit? Mañjuśrī replied, “Devaputra!”
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have four kinds of mind that can accomplish the cause and can accomplish the fruit.
What are the four? First, the initial resolve for enlightenment (prathamacittotpāda).
Second, the resolve of practice;
third, the non-retrogressive resolve;
and fourth, the resolve of the stage of being born only once more before attaining Buddhahood.
"Furthermore, O Devaputra!

The first production of the thought of enlightenment is like various seeds; the second, the production of the thought of practice, is like the sprouting and growth of a shoot; the third, the production of the thought of non-retrogression, is like the initial accomplishment of the stem, leaves, flowers, and fruit; and the fourth, the production of the thought of the stage of being born only once more before Buddhahood, is like the fruit and so forth being of practical use."
"Furthermore, O Devaputra!

The initial aspiration is like the carpenter’s wisdom in gathering materials; the second, the aspiration of practice, is like the wisdom of cutting and refining the timber; the third, the non-retrogressive aspiration, is like the wisdom of securely installing the materials; the fourth, the aspiration of the stage of one birth remaining (ekajātipratibaddha), is like the wisdom of the completed carriage carrying its load."

"Furthermore, O Son of Heaven! The initial aspiration is like the newly risen moon; the second, the aspiration of practice, is like the moon on the fifth day; the third, the aspiration of non-retrogression, is like the moon on the tenth day; the fourth, the aspiration of the stage of being born only once more before Buddhahood, is like the moon on the fourteenth day; and the wisdom of the Tathāgata is like the moon on the fifteenth day."
"Furthermore, O Son of Heaven!

The first resolve, the initial aspiration, can transcend the stage of the śrāvaka; the second resolve, the resolve of practice, can transcend the stage of the pratyekabuddha; the third resolve, the non-retrogressive resolve, can transcend the indeterminate stage; and the fourth resolve, the resolve of the stage of being born only once more before Buddhahood, abides securely in the determinate stage."
"Furthermore, O Devaputra!

The initial aspiration is like the knowledge of learning the first chapter; the second, the aspiration of practice, is like the knowledge that distinguishes all chapters; the third, the non-retrogressive aspiration, is like the knowledge of calculation; the fourth, the aspiration of the stage of being born only once more before Buddhahood, is like the knowledge that penetrates all treatises."
“Furthermore, O Devaputra!

The first resolve, the initial aspiration, arises from causes; the second, the resolve of practice, arises from wisdom; the third, the resolve of non-retrogression, arises from abandonment; and the fourth, the resolve of the stage of one birth remaining before Buddhahood, arises from the fruit.”
"Furthermore, O Devaputra!

The first arousal of the mind is comprised by causes; the second, the arousal of the mind of practice, is comprised by wisdom; the third, the irreversible arousal of the mind, is comprised by abandonment; and the fourth, the arousal of the mind of the stage of one birth remaining before Buddhahood, is comprised by the fruit."
"Furthermore, O Devaputra!

From the first production of the thought of enlightenment, the cause arises; from the second, the practice, the wisdom of the thought of enlightenment arises; from the third, the non-retrogressive production of the thought of enlightenment, the severance of arising arises; and from the fourth, the production of the thought of enlightenment of the stage of 'one birth remaining,' the fruit arises."
"Furthermore, O Devaputra!

First is the section on the distinctions of the causes for the initial arousal of the mind; second is the section on the distinctions of the wisdom for practicing the arousal of the mind; third is the section on the distinctions of severance for the non-retrogressive arousal of the mind; and fourth is the section on the distinctions of the fruits for the arousal of the mind at the stage of being one birth away from Buddhahood."
"Furthermore, O Devaputra!

The initial resolve is like the skillful means of gathering medicinal herbs; the second, the resolve of practice, is like the skillful means of identifying the medicinal herbs; the third, the non-retrogressive resolve, is like the skillful means of taking medicine when ill; the fourth, the resolve of the stage of being born only once more before Buddhahood, is like the skillful means of recovering from the illness."

"Furthermore, O Devaputra, first, one who has resolved to attain enlightenment studies as one born into the family of a Dharma King; second, one who has resolved to practice studies the Dharma of the Dharma King; third, one with the non-retrogressive resolve is able to fully master the Dharma of the Dharma King; fourth, one with the resolve of the stage of being born only once more before Buddhahood studies the Dharma of the Dharma King and attains sovereign mastery."

At that time, among the great assembly there was a devaputra named Śāntiprabhānātha, who had not regressed from his resolve for *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Then the devaputra Śāntiprabhānātha asked the Dharma-prince Mañjuśrī:
"What is the ultimate summary of the path for all Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas?"
"By means of this concise path, all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas swiftly attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. Mañjuśrī replied, "Devaputra!"
The abbreviated path of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas consists of two kinds; by means of these two paths, all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas swiftly attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
What are these two?
First, the path of skillful means;
second, the path of wisdom.

Skillful means is the knowledge of gathering wholesome dharmas; wisdom is the knowledge that knows all dharmas as they truly are. Furthermore, skillful means is observing all sentient beings; wisdom is the knowledge that is detached from all dharmas.
Furthermore, skillful means is knowing the correspondence of all dharmas; wisdom is the knowledge that all dharmas are non-correspondent.
Furthermore, skillful means is observing the path of causes; wisdom is the knowledge that extinguishes the path of causes.
Furthermore, skillful means is the knowledge of the distinctions among all phenomena, while wisdom is the knowledge that all phenomena are without distinction;
furthermore, skillful means is the adornment of Buddha-fields, while wisdom is the knowledge that the adornment of Buddha-fields is equal and without distinction;
furthermore, skillful means is entering into the faculties and activities of sentient beings, while wisdom is the knowledge that does not perceive sentient beings.
Furthermore, "skillful means" leads to the place of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), while "wisdom" enables one to realize the wisdom of all the Buddha’s *bodhi*-dharmas.
"Moreover, O Devaputra, there are two further concise paths for the Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas; by means of these two paths, the Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas swiftly attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."
What are these two?
First, the path of assistance;
second, the path of abandonment.
The five pāramitās are the path of assistance, while the prajñāpāramitā is the path of abandonment.
Furthermore, there are two kinds of concise paths. What are these two?
First is the path with obstruction;
second is the unobstructed path.
The path with obstruction refers to the five pāramitās; the unobstructed path refers to the prajñāpāramitā.
"Furthermore, there are two kinds of abbreviated paths.
What are the two? First, the path with outflows (sāsrava-mārga); [the second is the path without outflows (anāsrava-mārga)]."
Second is the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*).
The tainted path consists of the five *pāramitās*, while the untainted path consists of the *prajñāpāramitā*.
"Furthermore, there are two kinds of abbreviated paths."
What are these two?
First, the path with measure;
second, the immeasurable path.
The path with measure involves the conceptualization of signs, while the immeasurable path does not involve the conceptualization of signs.
Furthermore, there are two kinds of abbreviated paths. What are these two?
The first is the path of wisdom;
the second is the path of abandonment.
The path of wisdom refers to the stages from the first bhūmi through the seventh bhūmi; the path of abandonment refers to the stages from the eighth bhūmi through the tenth bhūmi.
At that time, there was a bodhisattva mahāsattva in the assembly named Vīryacaryājñāna, who asked the Dharma Prince Mañjuśrī:
“What is meant by the term ‘bodhisattva mahāsattva’?”
"What is meant by the wisdom of a bodhisattva-mahāsattva? Mañjuśrī replied, "Good son!..."
"Meaning is called non-correspondence; wisdom is called correspondence.
The Bodhisattva Valiant Practice of Wisdom said, "Mañjuśrī!..."
"What is meant by 'the name is dissociated from the meaning'?
What is meant by 'the wisdom is associated with the name'? Mañjuśrī replied:
“Good son! ‘Meaning’ (artha) refers to the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta). That meaning does not correspond with any single dharma, nor does it not correspond with any single dharma. Why is this?

Because they are without change and without marks, in terms of meaning, there is not a single dharma with which they are associated, nor is there a single dharma with which they are not associated. Since their meaning is fundamentally unestablished, there is therefore not a single dharma with which they are associated, nor a single dharma with which they are not associated.
"Meaning" (artha) is neither shifting nor increasing; there is not a single dharma with which it is associated, nor is there a single dharma with which it is not associated.
Good son, the wise call this "the Path" (mārga)!
The Way is that which is in mutual correspondence with the mind, not non-correspondence.
Good son! For this reason, wisdom is called "correspondence," not "non-correspondence."
"Furthermore, good son! Wisdom is defined as being associated with abandonment. Therefore, good son!"
Wisdom is defined as associated dharmas,
not dissociated dharmas. Furthermore, son of good family,
wisdom is defined as skillfully contemplating the five aggregates, the twelve bases, the eighteen elements, the twelve links of dependent origination, and what is possible and what is impossible.
Good son! For this reason, wisdom is called "concordant" and not "discordant. Furthermore, good son!
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas possess ten kinds of knowledge.
What are these ten? The first is the knowledge of causes.
Second, the wisdom of fruition;
third, the wisdom of meaning;
fourth, the wisdom of skillful means;
Fifth, the wisdom of insight;
sixth, the wisdom of integration;
seventh, the wisdom of the perfections;
Eighth, the wisdom of great compassion;
ninth, the wisdom of teaching and transforming sentient beings;
tenth, the wisdom of non-attachment to all phenomena.
"Good son! These are called the ten kinds of knowledge of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
Furthermore, good son!"
All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have ten kinds of arousal. What are the ten?
First is the arousal of the body, because they desire to bring the bodily karma of all sentient beings to purity.
Second is the arousal [of the mind] through speech, because one desires to bring about the purification of the vocal karma of all sentient beings;
third is the arousal [of the mind] through thought, because one desires to bring about the purification of the mental karma of all sentient beings;
fourth is the internal arousal, because one does not engage in false discrimination regarding any sentient beings.
Fifth is the arousal of external manifestation, because of practicing with equanimity toward all sentient beings;
sixth is the arousal of wisdom, because of being fully endowed with the purity of Buddha-wisdom;
seventh is the arousal of the pure land, because of demonstrating the meritorious adornments of all Buddha-lands.
Eighth, the resolve to teach and transform sentient beings, because of knowing the medicine for all the diseases of affliction;
ninth, the genuine resolve, because of accomplishing the assembly of concentration;
tenth, the resolve of a mind satisfied with unconditioned wisdom, because of non-attachment to all three realms.
“Good son! These are called the ten kinds of aspirations of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas. Furthermore, good son!”
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have ten kinds of practices. What are these ten?
First, the practice of the pāramitās;
Second, the practice of gathering [disciples];
third, the practice of wisdom;
fourth, the practice of skillful means.
Fifth, the practice of great compassion;
sixth, the practice of seeking the dharma of aiding wisdom;
seventh, the practice of seeking the dharma of aiding knowledge;
Eighth, the practice of mental purity;
ninth, the practice of contemplating the truths;
tenth, the practice of non-attachment toward all things pleasant and unpleasant.
"Good son! These are called the ten kinds of practices of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas. Furthermore, good son!"
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have eleven kinds of inexhaustible contemplations.
What are these eleven? First, the inexhaustible contemplation of the body; [and so forth].
Second, the contemplation of the inexhaustibility of phenomena;
third, the contemplation of the inexhaustibility of afflictions;
fourth, the contemplation of the inexhaustibility of dharmas.
Fifth, the contemplation on the inexhaustibility of craving;
sixth, the contemplation on the inexhaustibility of views;
seventh, the contemplation on the inexhaustibility of the factors conducive to enlightenment;
Eighth, the contemplation of grasping the inexhaustible;
ninth, the contemplation of non-attachment to the inexhaustible;
tenth, the contemplation of correspondence with the inexhaustible.
Eleventh is the contemplation on the inexhaustible nature of wisdom at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*). Good son,
these are called the eleven kinds of inexhaustible contemplations of the Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas.
"Furthermore, good son, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have ten kinds of remedial dharmas. What are these ten?
First, it counteracts the mind of stinginess and greed by raining down the rain of giving;
second, it counteracts the mind of breaking precepts by purifying the three dharmas of body, speech, and mental action;
third, it counteracts the mind of anger by practicing pure great compassion.
Fourth, it counteracts the mind of indolence, because one seeks all Buddha-dharmas without weariness;
fifth, it counteracts the mind of unwholesome applied and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*), because one attains the mastery and spontaneity of meditative concentration and liberation;
sixth, it counteracts the mind of delusion, because it gives rise to the skillful means of wisdom that aids in definitive certainty.
Seventh, it counteracts the mind of various afflictions by giving rise to the factors that assist the path;
eighth, it counteracts the path of perversion by gathering the factors that assist the true truths and giving rise to the non-perverted path;
ninth, it counteracts the lack of mastery by attaining mastery over the appropriate and inappropriate times for the Dharma.
Tenth, as an antidote to the mark of selfhood, they contemplate all phenomena as being without self.
Son of good family!
These are called the ten kinds of remedial dharmas of the Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas.
"Furthermore, good son, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have ten kinds of stages of tranquility (*śāntabhūmi*). What are these ten?
First is tranquility of body, because of being free from the three kinds of unwholesome bodily actions;
second is tranquility of speech, because of purifying the four kinds of vocal actions;
third is tranquility of mind, because of being free from the three kinds of mental misconduct.
Fourth is inner tranquility, because of non-attachment to one's own body;
fifth is tranquility regarding external objects, because of non-attachment to all phenomena;
sixth is tranquility regarding the merit of wisdom, because of non-attachment to the path.
Seventh is supreme tranquility, because of observing the noble stages as they truly are;
eighth is tranquility reaching the limits of the future, because of supporting practice with the wisdom that reaches the other shore;
ninth is tranquility regarding worldly affairs, because of not deceiving any sentient beings.
Tenth, they do not cherish their own bodies or minds because they teach and transform all sentient beings with great compassion.
Son of good family!
These are called the ten stages of tranquility of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas.
"Furthermore, good son!
All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas attain awakening by practicing according to reality; they do not attain awakening by practicing contrary to reality."
"Good son! What is called the 'practice of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas according to reality'? Good son!"
One who practices according to reality is able to act as they speak; one who does not practice according to reality possesses only words, for they are unable to practice in accordance with reality.
"Furthermore, good son! Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have another two kinds of practice in accordance with reality. What are these two?
First is the path of practicing according to reality through wisdom;
second is the path of practicing according to reality through abandonment. Good son!
This is called the two kinds of practice according to reality for all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
Furthermore, son of good family,
there are again two kinds of practice according to reality for all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
What are these two?
First, the practice of subduing oneself according to reality;
second, the practice of teaching and transforming sentient beings according to reality.
“Good son! These are called the two kinds of practice according to reality for all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
Furthermore, good son!”
Furthermore, there are two kinds of practice according to reality for all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas. What are these two?
First, the practice according to reality through the wisdom of effortful application; [and second, the practice according to reality through effortless spontaneity].
Second is the practice of non-effortful wisdom as it truly is.
Son of good family!
These are called the two kinds of practice as it truly is for all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
"Furthermore, good son! Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have another two kinds of practice according to reality. What are these two?
First, skillfully knowing how to distinguish the various stages and practicing accordingly as they truly are;
second, skillfully knowing the expedient means that are without differentiation among the stages and practicing accordingly as they truly are.
"Noble son! These are called the two kinds of authentic practice of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
Furthermore, noble son!"

Furthermore, there are two kinds of practice according to reality for all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas. What are these two? First, the practice according to reality that is free from the faults of the stages; second, the practice according to reality that is free from the faults of the paths. What is the practice according to reality that is free from the faults of the stages? It refers to the practice according to reality by which a bodhisattva-mahāsattva, having already entered the first stage, does not fall back into the level of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, nor does he fall into the errors of the views of non-Buddhists. This is called the practice according to reality that is free from the faults of the stages. What is the practice according to reality that is free from the faults of the paths? It refers to the practice according to reality by which a bodhisattva-mahāsattva, having already attained the path of seeing, does not fall back into the level of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, nor does he fall into the errors of the views of non-Buddhists. Second, they skillfully know the methods for transitioning from stage to stage and practice accordingly in accordance with reality. Good son,
these are called the two kinds of practice in accordance with reality for Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas.
"Furthermore, good son! Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have another two kinds of practice according to reality. What are these two?
First, the ability to explain the practice of the stages of the śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha as they truly are;
second, skillfully knowing the expedient means for non-retrogression from the Buddha’s bodhi and practicing them as they truly are.
"Good son! These are called the two kinds of practice according to reality for all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas. Good son!"
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas possess such immeasurable and boundless practices of reality as these; all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should train in this way in the practice of reality.
If bodhisattva-mahāsattvas can practice reality in this manner, they will swiftly attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi without it being difficult for them.
At that time, the Buddha praised the Dharma Prince Mañjuśrī, saying: “Excellent, excellent, Mañjuśrī!”
"You have now skillfully expounded the path of original karma for all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas; it is exactly as you have said.
When this Dharma was spoken, ten thousand bodhisattvas attained the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).

Mañjuśrī the Dharma Prince and all others in the world—gods, humans, asuras, and so forth—hearing what the Buddha had spoken, were all greatly rejoiced; they believed, accepted, and practiced it accordingly.
